title: Jatakas as Moral Arguments
bigQuestion: How do the Jataka stories argue for a way of life, and what do readers do when a story's hero troubles them?

story.title: A Day for Vessantara
story.kicker: A village in northeastern Thailand gathers from before dawn to hear one long story from beginning to end.
paragraphs: In many villages in northeastern Thailand, one festival each year is given to a single story. People call it Bun Phawet. The temple hall is hung with painted cloth scrolls showing scene after scene. Families bring food for the monks. Children run between the pillars.

Before dawn, the recitation begins. Monks take turns reading the story of Prince Vessantara aloud, one chapter each, often in a singing style. There are thirteen chapters in the Thai telling, and together they hold about a thousand verses. The reading can last all day and into the night.

The listeners know the story well. Vessantara, a generous prince, gives away a magic elephant, his wealth, his chariot, and finally his own two children and his wife. Some listeners cry at the scene where the children are led away. Many say that hearing the whole story in one day brings great merit.

The Vessantara Jataka is the last and longest of the 547 Jatakas in the Pali collection. Buddhists tell it as the Buddha's last human life before the one in which he awakened. It is also the most debated. This chapter reads the Jatakas as arguments: stories built to show what a way of life looks like.
story.think: Why might a community honor a story that also makes some of its listeners cry out in protest?

lessons.title: Present, Past, Identification
lessons.mainIdea: Each Jataka in the Pali collection has a frame: a story of the present, a story of the past, and a closing identification.
reading: The Pali collection holds 547 *Jataka* tales. Each one is set in a frame with three parts. First comes the story of the present: something happens among the Buddha's monks, and he is asked about it. Then comes the story of the past: the Buddha tells of an event in one of his former lives. Last comes the identification.

In the identification, the Buddha, as the text presents him, names who was who. The wise hare, he says, was I. The foolish monkey was a certain monk. The kind king was my father. The frame ties the old story to the people listening, and it teaches that lives connect through *karma* and rebirth, as Buddhists believe.

Only the verses of the Jatakas are counted as canonical in the Theravada Pali Canon. The prose stories around them come from a commentary, the Jatakatthavannana, compiled in Sri Lanka around the fifth century CE. The Cowell edition, translated by several scholars between 1895 and 1907, puts both into English and is in the public domain.

words.d: a story of one of the Buddha's former lives, as Buddhists tell it
an outer story that holds an inner story, as the present holds the past in a Jataka
the Jataka's ending, where the Buddha names who each character was
intentional action and its results; kamma in Pali

lessons.title: Stories That Argue
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars read Jatakas as moral arguments: each one sets up a situation and shows a quality at work.
reading: A fable often ends with a moral stated in one line. A Jataka does more. It sets up a hard situation, puts a character in it, and shows what that character chooses and what follows. The reader sees a quality in action. In this sense the story is an *argument*: it gives reasons, through events, for living a certain way.

Many Jatakas were told before the Buddha's time as folk tales. Scholars think Buddhist storytellers took some of them and added the frame. The same animal fable might appear in the Panchatantra, a Sanskrit collection of animal tales, and in the Jatakas, with different lessons drawn. The frame turns a folk tale into a Buddhist teaching.

Monks use Jatakas in sermons. Artists paint them on temple walls. Parents tell them at bedtime. Scholars such as Naomi Appleton, in Jataka Stories in Theravada Buddhism (2010), study how the stories teach about the path of a *bodhisatta*, a being on the way to Buddhahood.

words.d: reasons for a claim; a story can argue by showing choices and results
Pali for bodhisattva: in Jatakas, the future Buddha in his former lives
an ancient Sanskrit collection of animal fables, some shared with the Jatakas

lessons.title: Ten Perfections
lessons.mainIdea: Theravada tradition lists ten perfections, and the last ten great Jatakas are often matched to them one by one.
reading: Theravada Buddhists speak of ten *paramis*, or perfections. These are qualities a bodhisatta develops across many lives. They are generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness and equanimity. Mahayana texts list six or ten paramitas, overlapping but not identical.

The last ten Jatakas in the Pali collection, called the Mahanipata or great birth stories, are long and carefully told. Thai and other Theravada traditions match each of them with one perfection. Temuiya, the silent prince, shows renunciation. Mahajanaka, who swims for seven days, shows energy. Vessantara, the last, shows *generosity*.

These ten are hugely popular in Southeast Asia. They are painted in sequence on temple walls, acted in dance and puppet theater, and printed in picture books. Buddhists believe the future Buddha perfected each quality before his final life. The stories show those qualities at their highest pitch, which is part of why some are so hard to read.

words.d: a perfection: a quality the bodhisatta develops across many lives; paramita in Sanskrit
dana: giving freely; the first of the ten perfections
the ten great Jatakas that end the Pali collection

lessons.title: The Hare in the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: In the Hare Jataka, a hare with nothing to give offers his own body to a hungry guest, showing generosity at its limit.
reading: Jataka no. 316, the Sasa Jataka, tells of four friends in a forest: a hare, a monkey, a jackal and an otter. They agree to give food on a holy day. The otter finds fish, the jackal finds meat and curd, and the monkey brings mangoes. The hare eats only grass. He has nothing a guest could eat.

So the hare resolves that if a guest comes, he will give his own body. Sakka, king of the gods in the story, disguises himself as a hungry brahmin to test him. The hare tells him to build a fire and leaps in. The fire does not burn him. Sakka reveals himself and paints the hare's image on the moon, so all may see it.

Read closely, the story makes a claim about *dana*, giving. The gift that counts most is the one that costs the giver most. The hare is the Buddha, the identification says. Buddhists in Japan, China and elsewhere still point to the hare in the moon. Many readers find the story beautiful; some ask whether any gift should cost this much.

words.d: giving or generosity; a central Buddhist practice
king of the gods in Buddhist stories; Indra in Hindu texts
Jataka no. 316, the story of the hare who offered himself

lessons.title: The Monkey King's Bridge
lessons.mainIdea: In the Mahakapi Jataka, a monkey king makes his own body a bridge to save his troop, and a human king learns what ruling means.
reading: Jataka no. 407, the Mahakapi Jataka, tells of a monkey king who leads eighty thousand monkeys. They live in a great mango tree by the Ganges. A human king, the king of Benares, wants the mangoes and orders his archers to surround the tree at night. The monkeys are trapped.

The monkey king leaps across the river, ties a bamboo cane to his foot and leaps back, but the cane is too short. He grips a branch and makes his own body the last span. The troop runs across his back to safety. One monkey, who is jealous, jumps hard on his back and breaks it. The king of Benares sees it all.

Moved, the human king has the monkey lowered and cared for. Before he dies, the monkey king explains his choice: a ruler should seek the welfare of those he rules. The human king honors him with a royal funeral. The story is a *political* argument as well as a moral one: it shows a ruler who serves his people with his body.

words.d: Jataka no. 407, the story of the great monkey king who became a bridge
health, safety and good of a group
about rulers, power and how communities are governed

look.title: Two Kings
look.text: The human king sends archers for mangoes. The monkey king lets his troop run across his back. At the end, the human king kneels by the dying monkey and asks why he did it. The monkey answers as one ruler to another.
look.prompt: What does the human king learn? Why might a story put this lesson in a monkey's mouth?

check.q: What lesson does the monkey king give the human king?

check.q: Why can the story be called a political argument?

check.why: It contrasts two rulers and shows service as the mark of good rule.

lessons.title: The Story in Brief
lessons.mainIdea: Prince Vessantara gives away his kingdom's rain-making elephant, his wealth, his children and his wife, and all are restored in the end.
reading: Jataka no. 547 opens with a prince who loves to give. Vessantara gives away his kingdom's white elephant, which brings rain. The people are furious, and he is banished with his wife Maddi and their two children, Jali and Kanhajina. On the road, he gives away his horses and chariot. The family settles in a mountain hermitage.

One day, while Maddi is out gathering food, an old brahmin named Jujaka arrives and asks for the children as servants. Vessantara gives them. The children hide in a pond and plead, but he gives them anyway. Then Sakka, disguised as a brahmin, asks for Maddi. Vessantara gives her too. Sakka at once returns her and blesses him.

In the end, the children are brought to their grandfather, the king, who ransoms them. Jujaka dies from overeating. The family is reunited and Vessantara is called home to rule. The earth shakes at each great gift, the story says. Buddhists tell it as the last life of the bodhisatta before his birth as *Siddhattha*.

words.d: the prince of Jataka no. 547, who gives away everything, told as the Buddha's last human life before his final one
Vessantara's wife, who follows him into exile
the personal name of the Buddha before awakening; Siddhartha in Sanskrit

lessons.title: An Old Debate
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists and others have argued over Vessantara's gift of his family for about two thousand years, and they answer in several ways.
reading: The gift of the children has troubled readers from early on. The Questions of King Milinda, a Pali text from around the start of the common era, has the king ask the monk Nagasena whether Vessantara did wrong. Nagasena defends the gift as the act of a bodhisatta who sought awakening for the good of all. The question shows the debate is ancient.

Modern readers answer in several ways. Some Buddhist teachers stress that the story is about perfect non-attachment, not ordinary family life, and is not a model for parents. Some point out that the story itself lets Maddi and the children voice their grief, which takes the pain seriously. Scholars such as Steven Collins have argued the story is meant to be felt as hard.

In Thailand and Laos, many listeners weep at the children's scenes and still honor Vessantara. Some women in the audience, ethnographers report, identify with Maddi. A few modern critics call the story harmful. A careful student reports these readings without choosing one. The goal is to understand how a *community* holds a hard story.

words.d: not clinging to people, things or outcomes; a Buddhist ideal
Milindapanha: a Pali dialogue between the Greek king Menander and the monk Nagasena
the people who share a practice and keep a story alive

look.title: Four Readers
look.text: Nagasena: the gift served the good of all beings. A Thai grandmother: I cry for Maddi every year, and I honor him. A modern teacher: this is about letting go, not about parenting. A critic: no ideal justifies giving away children.
look.prompt: Which reader pays most attention to the story's own details? Explain without judging who is right.

check.q: Which early text shows the Vessantara debate is old?
check.why: King Milinda asks Nagasena whether Vessantara did wrong.

check.q: How does Nagasena defend Vessantara?
choices: By saying the story is false

check.why: Nagasena presents the gift as part of the bodhisatta path.

check.q: What is a fair way to describe how Buddhists respond to the gift of the children?
choices: They respond in several ways, and many both weep and honor him

check.why: Responses range from defense to grief to critique, often within one audience.

lessons.title: Bharhut
lessons.mainIdea: Carvings at the stupa of Bharhut, from about the second century BCE, are among the oldest pictures of Jataka stories, and some name them.
reading: Bharhut is a site in central India where a great stupa once stood. Its stone railings and gateways, carved around the second century BCE, show many scenes. Some are Jatakas. Several carvings carry short inscriptions that name the story, which lets scholars match pictures to texts.

This matters for dating. If a Jataka is carved and named at Bharhut, a form of that story was known by then. Scholars use Bharhut and the similar site at Sanchi to show that Jataka telling is old. The carvings also show that some stories differed from the later written versions.

Most of the Bharhut railing is now in the Indian Museum in Kolkata. Visitors can see the *relief* carvings up close. Among them is a scene scholars identify as the Mahakapi Jataka: a monkey stretched across a river while others cross. The stone tells the story without words.

words.d: a stupa site in central India with carvings from about the second century BCE
a carving that stands out from a flat stone surface
words cut into stone or metal

lessons.title: Borobudur
lessons.mainIdea: Borobudur in Java, built around 800 CE, carries hundreds of carved panels, many of them Jataka and related stories.
reading: Borobudur, on the island of Java in Indonesia, is one of the largest Buddhist monuments in the world. It was built around the late eighth and early ninth centuries CE under the Sailendra dynasty. It rises in terraces, with walls of carved panels along the galleries.

Buddhist pilgrims walk around the monument clockwise, climbing level by level. As they walk, the panels tell stories: the Buddha's life, Jatakas and avadanas, and scenes from Mahayana sutras such as the Gandavyuha. Scholars count about 1,460 narrative panels. The walk itself is a kind of reading.

Borobudur was restored with UNESCO's help in the 1970s and named a World Heritage Site in 1991. Buddhists from Indonesia and abroad gather there for *Vesak* each year. The monument shows how Jataka tales traveled far from India and were retold in stone for new audiences.

words.d: a great Buddhist monument in Java, Indonesia, built c. 800 CE
a Buddhist story about the deeds of a person and their results
a festival many Buddhists keep for the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing
